en: To exist in very large numbers; to be plentiful
hook: A-BOUND-less supply: so much that there's no boundary.
story: Abound. Every June, Ishita's grandmother in Rajshahi calls with the same warning: "Bring empty bags." Mangoes abound. They pile up on rooftops, roll under beds, fill every bucket in the house, until neighbours start leaving them on strangers' doorsteps at night. You cannot walk ten steps without stepping on one. That is what abound means: to exist in huge numbers, more than anyone needs. On the GRE, when a passage says errors abound in a theory, picture Rajshahi in June.

gre.s: Far from being scarce, allusions to the ancient epic ____ in the poet's later work, surfacing in nearly every stanza.
gre.clue: Far from being scarce

en: Without a clear shape, form, or structure
hook: A-MORPH-ous: 'a' means without, 'morph' means shape. Without shape.
story: Amorphous. Zayan's study plan began as a cloud of good intentions: "Study vocab sometime. Maybe math too." No days. No targets. No shape at all. A week later he had learned exactly nine words. His sister grabbed a marker and drew a grid on his wall: thirty words each morning, one quant set each night. The cloud became a staircase. Amorphous means having no clear shape or structure, like smoke you cannot hold. An amorphous plan is just a wish.

gre.s: The committee's proposal remained frustratingly ____: it gestured toward reform but specified no budget, no timeline, and no responsible agency.
gre.clue: specified no budget, no timeline, and no responsible agency

en: Very strict or serious; extremely plain, without comfort or decoration
hook: AUSTERE sounds like 'a stair' of bare concrete: no carpet, no decoration, just hard steps.
story: Austere. When Rafi visited his grandfather's room for the first time, he looked for the TV. There was none. One wooden chair. One lamp. A shelf with three books. Rice and lentils, every single day, and not a single picture on the walls. "Don't you get bored, Dada?" Rafi asked. The old man smiled. "Less to own, less to worry about." Austere means severely plain and strict, with every comfort stripped away. An austere life, an austere building, an austere teacher.

gre.s: In contrast to the lavish palaces of his predecessors, the new ruler's residence was strikingly ____, furnished with little more than a desk and a cot.
gre.clue: In contrast to the lavish palaces

en: To give a false impression of; to hide the truth behind an appearance
bn: ভুল ধারণা দেওয়া; আসল রূপ আড়াল করা
hook: BE-LIE: the appearance tells a LIE about what's underneath.
story: Belie. Tanvir walked out of the GRE center grinning and waving at his friends. "How was it?" they shouted. "Easy!" But in the rickshaw home, he put his head in his hands. He was sure he had failed the quant section. His cheerful face had told a lie about what he really felt. That is belie: an outward appearance that gives a false picture of the truth underneath. Remember it as be-lie: the surface tells a lie.

gre.s: The pianist's relaxed, almost careless stage manners ____ the punishing hours of practice that lie behind every performance.
gre.clue: relaxed, almost careless

en: Changing mood or behavior suddenly and unpredictably
hook: CAPRICIOUS sounds like a CAPRI goat: it jumps randomly from rock to rock.
story: Capricious. Two days before her GRE, Nadia looked up at the Dhaka sky. Sunshine at breakfast. A thunderstorm by lunch. Blazing heat by four, and rain again at dinner. "This weather cannot make up its mind," she sighed. That is exactly what capricious means: changing suddenly, for no clear reason. A capricious boss praises you on Monday and shouts at you on Tuesday. So when a GRE passage calls something capricious, think of April in Dhaka: unpredictable, impulsive, impossible to plan for.

gre.s: Investors grew wary of the regulator, whose rulings seemed ____, reversing course from month to month without any stated rationale.
gre.clue: reversing course from month to month without any stated rationale

en: Intellectual rather than emotional or physical; related to the brain
hook: CEREBRAL = cerebrum, the thinking part of the brain.
story: Cerebral. Sara picked the movie for family night: a slow mystery where every clue was hidden in conversation. Ten minutes in, her little brother was asleep. Forty minutes in, her father was checking cricket scores. Sara, meanwhile, was scribbling theories in a notebook. "Your movies are too cerebral," her brother groaned afterward. "They make my brain hurt." Cerebral means appealing to the intellect rather than to emotion or the senses. Think of the cerebrum, the thinking part of the brain.

gre.s: Critics who expected a stirring, emotional drama found the film disappointingly ____, more interested in testing the audience's logic than in moving its heart.
gre.clue: more interested in testing the audience's logic than in moving its heart

en: Pleasant and friendly; well suited to one's taste or nature
hook: CON-GENIAL: comes with a GENIAL, friendly feeling.
story: Congenial. After two lonely months studying in her room, Mitu finally joined a GRE study group at a café in Dhanmondi. She was nervous. But the members passed her their best notes, laughed at her terrible mnemonics, and ordered an extra cup of tea for her without asking. By the end of the evening she felt she had known them for years. Congenial means pleasant, friendly, and well suited to you. A congenial place makes it easy to be yourself.

gre.s: Although the two scientists had been bitter rivals in print, they found each other surprisingly ____ in person, chatting amiably for hours.
gre.clue: chatting amiably for hours

en: Standing out clearly; easy to notice
hook: CON-SPIC-uous: SPIC sounds like 'spec', as in spectacle. Everyone can see it.
story: Conspicuous. Everyone at the wedding wore soft pastel colours. Then Arif walked in wearing a bright orange suit. Heads turned. Aunties whispered. The photographer kept pointing his camera at him by mistake. Even the bride glanced over twice. Arif simply could not be missed. Conspicuous means standing out so clearly that everyone notices. If you want to be conspicuous, wear orange to a pastel wedding. If you want to be inconspicuous, wear beige and stand near the snacks.

gre.s: The detective was puzzled that the thief had chosen such a ____ getaway car, a bright yellow convertible that half the town would remember.
gre.clue: half the town would remember

en: Done quickly and without attention to detail
hook: CURSORY: like moving your CURSOR quickly down a page without reading.
story: Cursory. Ten minutes before the exam, Farhan flipped through fifty pages of notes in two minutes, his eyes skating over the headings. He felt ready. Then question one asked about a formula he had only skimmed past, and his mind went blank. A cursory look is quick and superficial, like sliding your cursor down a page without reading. Cursory reviews miss details. The GRE rewards careful reading, not cursory glances.

gre.s: Because the inspector gave the bridge only a ____ examination, glancing at it from his car, the cracks in its supports went unnoticed.
gre.clue: glancing at it from his car

en: Seeming difficult or intimidating enough to discourage you
hook: DAUNTING sounds like 'DON'T even try', which is what the task seems to say.
story: Daunting. On the first night, Lamia opened the GRE word list and scrolled. And scrolled. And scrolled. More than a thousand words, many of them impossible to pronounce. Her stomach dropped. She almost closed the laptop for good. Then her brother said, "Don't climb the mountain. Climb one step." She split the list into groups of thirty, and the mountain became a staircase. Daunting means so difficult that it frightens you before you even begin.

gre.s: Though the task of cataloguing ten thousand manuscripts seemed ____ at first, the archivists found it manageable once they divided the work.
gre.clue: found it manageable once they divided the work

en: To treat or worship someone as a god
bn: দেবতা জ্ঞান করা; দেবত্ব আরোপ করা
hook: DEI-fy: 'dei' means god, as in deity. To make into a god.
story: Deify. When the young batsman scored a century in his first World Cup, fans went wild. Within a week his face was painted on rickshaws, printed on tea cups, and hung above shop counters with garlands of flowers. People refused to hear a single word against him. One uncle even lit a candle before every match. To deify someone is to treat them like a god, worshipping them far beyond what any human deserves. Deity means god; deify means to make one.

gre.s: Biographers who used to ____ the inventor now acknowledge his flaws, presenting him as a brilliant but very human figure.
gre.clue: now acknowledge his flaws

en: Intended to teach a lesson, often in a preachy or moralizing way
hook: DIDACTIC: 'DID you get the lesson? ACT on it!' says the preachy teacher.
story: Didactic. Uncle Karim's bedtime stories always ended the same way. The lazy rabbit lost. The honest woodcutter won. And then, just as the children were drifting off, he would raise one finger: "And the lesson is…" They groaned every time. His stories were didactic: designed mainly to teach a moral, often in a preachy way. On the GRE, a didactic tone means the author is lecturing the reader rather than simply telling a story.

gre.s: Readers who prefer subtlety may find the novel overly ____, since its author seldom misses a chance to spell out the moral of each chapter.
gre.clue: seldom misses a chance to spell out the moral

en: To spread information or ideas widely
hook: DIS-SEMIN-ate: 'semin' is Latin for seed. Scattering seeds in every direction.
story: Disseminate. At nine in the evening, the university quietly moved the final exam forward by one week. By nine thirty, the student union had disseminated the news everywhere: Facebook posts, WhatsApp groups, phone calls, and notices taped to every hostel door. By midnight, even students in distant villages knew. To disseminate is to spread information widely, the way a farmer scatters seeds across a whole field so they land everywhere at once.

gre.s: Public health officials worked to ____ accurate information about the virus as quickly as rumors were spreading online.
gre.clue: as quickly as rumors were spreading

en: Possible and practical to do
hook: FEASIBLE: is it EASY-ble? If it can be done, it's feasible.
story: Feasible. "I will learn all the GRE words in one week," Arif announced. His mentor laughed gently. "That is not feasible. But thirty words a day for five weeks? That is feasible." Arif tried the second plan, and five weeks later he knew every word. Feasible means possible and practical to actually carry out, given your time and resources. Before any big plan, ask yourself: is this feasible, or is it just a dream?

gre.s: Engineers concluded that the bridge, though elegant on paper, was not ____ given the region's budget and the instability of its soil.
gre.clue: given the region's budget and the instability of its soil

en: To openly disregard a rule, law, or custom
hook: FLOUT the rule, FLAUNT the attitude: breaking it proudly in public.
story: Flout. The sign at the exam hall door was huge and red: No Phones. One candidate sat in the waiting room, scrolling openly, laughing at videos while the guard watched him. He was not hiding anything. He simply did not care. To flout a rule is to break it boldly and in public, as if it does not exist. Do not confuse it with flaunt, which means to show off. You flout the rules; you flaunt your new watch.

gre.s: Rather than quietly ignoring the dress code, the students chose to ____ it openly, arriving in costumes that mocked the regulations.
gre.clue: Rather than quietly ignoring

en: Of the same kind; uniform throughout
hook: HOMO = same, GENE = kind. Same kind all through.
story: Homogeneous. Priya's mother stood over the cake batter, stirring and stirring. "Not yet," she said. "I can still see lumps." She kept going until every spoonful looked exactly the same: smooth, golden, no streaks of flour anywhere. "Now it is homogeneous." Homogeneous means uniform throughout, made of parts that are all alike. Homo means same, genus means kind. Its opposite is heterogeneous, which means mixed and varied, like a fruit salad.

gre.s: Once thought to be culturally ____, the region turns out to have been a patchwork of distinct languages and customs.
gre.clue: turns out to have been a patchwork

en: Dull and boring because of being routine
hook: HUM-DRUM: the same humming drumbeat, over and over.
story: Humdrum. Wake up. Bus. Office. Spreadsheet. Lunch. Spreadsheet. Bus. Sleep. Repeat. For three years, every day of Kamal's job was the same dull drumbeat. Hum, drum, hum, drum. Nothing ever changed. Then he started preparing for the GRE, and suddenly his evenings had a purpose: a scholarship, a new country, a new life. Humdrum means boringly ordinary and routine, lacking any excitement or variety. It even sounds like the dull, repeating beat it describes.

gre.s: Although the novelist's plots involve ordinary people with ____ jobs, her vivid prose makes even their daily routines seem thrilling.
gre.clue: even their daily routines

en: Lacking flavor; dull and uninteresting
hook: IN-SIPID: when you SIP it, there's no taste IN it.
story: Insipid. The hostel dal was famous. Not for its taste, but for its lack of taste. Watery, pale, no salt, no spice, nothing. Students joked that it tasted like warm rain. Joya added chili, lemon, and pickle, and it still tasted of nothing. Insipid means lacking flavour: when you sip it, there is no taste in it. The word also describes people, books, or lectures with no spark at all. An insipid speech puts the audience to sleep.

gre.s: The reviewer praised the soup's vivid spices but dismissed the dessert as ____, a sugary pudding with no discernible flavor.
gre.clue: with no discernible flavor

en: Talking a lot; very talkative
hook: LOQUACIOUS: 'loqu' means speak, as in eloquent. A loquacious person never stops speaking.
story: Loquacious. Rafi took a rickshaw to the station, a ten-minute ride. In those ten minutes, the driver told him about his village, his daughter's exam results, the price of rice, his opinion of every politician in the country, and a long story about a goat. Rafi said exactly one word: "Okay." The driver was loquacious: talking constantly and easily, sometimes charmingly, sometimes exhaustingly. Loqu means to speak, as in eloquent. The opposite is taciturn.

gre.s: The usually ____ host surprised his guests by sitting in silence for most of the dinner, barely contributing a sentence.
gre.clue: surprised his guests by sitting in silence

en: Disliking and distrusting people in general
hook: MIS = hate, ANTHROP = human. Hating humans.
story: Misanthropic. Old Mr. Haque lived alone at the end of the lane. When children played cricket, he slammed his windows. He refused every wedding invitation and muttered that people were selfish, noisy, and stupid. Yet every morning he fed the stray cats, talking to them softly. He disliked humans, not animals. That is misanthropic: distrusting and disliking humanity in general. Mis means hate, anthrop means human. The opposite is a philanthropist, who loves people and gives generously.

gre.s: The writer's later essays reveal a deeply ____ outlook; she came to regard human nature as fundamentally selfish and cruel.
gre.clue: regard human nature as fundamentally selfish and cruel

en: A wrong or misleading name
hook: MIS-NOMER: a MIStaken NAME (nomen means name).
story: Misnomer. The shop sign proudly said Super Fast Internet Café. Imran sat down, clicked a link, and waited. And waited. Three minutes for a single page. "Super fast?" he laughed. The name was a misnomer: a name that does not fit the thing it describes. A koala bear is not a bear. A peanut is not a nut. Mis means wrong, nomer means name. A misnomer is a mistaken label.

gre.s: Calling the archipelago's rainy season a monsoon is something of a ____, since the storms there arise from an entirely different weather system.
gre.clue: arise from an entirely different weather system

en: Failing to take proper care; careless about duty
hook: NEGLIGENT: someone who NEGLECTS their duty.
story: Negligent. The night guard at the garment factory had one job: check the fire alarms and keep the gate secure. Instead, he slept every night on a plastic chair, the gate wide open, the alarm batteries long dead. When a small fire broke out, nobody heard a thing until the smoke reached the street. The inquiry called him negligent: failing to take the care that your duty requires. Negligent people neglect their responsibilities.

gre.s: The court ruled that the landlord had been ____, since he had ignored repeated warnings about the building's faulty wiring.
gre.clue: ignored repeated warnings

en: Too eager to please or obey; excessively flattering
hook: OBSEQUIOUS: 'obsessively SEEK to please us'.
story: Obsequious. Whenever the manager walked past, Babu jumped to his feet. "Sir! Lovely tie, sir! Tea, sir? Your idea this morning was brilliant, sir!" He laughed at the manager's jokes before the punchline. He agreed before the manager finished speaking. His colleagues rolled their eyes. Obsequious means far too eager to please and obey, flattering in a way that feels fake. Think: obsessively seeking approval. It is the opposite of independent and self-respecting.

gre.s: The courtiers' ____ praise of the king, which never wavered even when his decrees were absurd, revealed more fear than admiration.
gre.clue: never wavered even when his decrees were absurd

en: To calm someone's anger by doing something to please them
hook: PLACATE: give a PLATE of food to calm someone down.
story: Placate. Mitu came home three hours late, phone dead, and found her mother standing at the door, arms crossed. Silence. Mitu apologized. Then she held out a box of her mother's favourite roshogolla and promised to call next time, every time. Slowly, very slowly, her mother's face softened, and she took a sweet. To placate is to calm someone's anger by giving them something they want. Think: hand them a plate of sweets.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ the furious shareholders, the board announced a generous dividend just days after the scandal broke.
gre.clue: furious shareholders

en: A natural tendency to do something, often something bad
hook: PRO-CLIVITY: like a slope (declivity) you naturally slide down.
story: Proclivity. Give Zayan a week for any assignment, and he will start it the night before. Every time. School essays, university reports, even his own birthday invitations. His friends no longer ask. "It is just who he is." A proclivity is a natural, habitual tendency to do something, often something you would be better off avoiding. Think of a slope: some people naturally slide toward the same habit again and again.

gre.s: Despite his ____ for risky investments, the financier surprised colleagues by keeping his own savings in government bonds.
gre.clue: surprised colleagues

en: Childishly silly and immature
hook: PUERILE: 'puer' means boy in Latin. Acting like a little boy.
story: Puerile. The quarterly meeting was serious: budgets, targets, possible layoffs. Then two senior managers in the back row started flicking paper balls at each other, giggling like ten-year-olds. The director stopped mid-sentence. "Gentlemen," she said coldly, "this behaviour is puerile." Puerile means childishly silly in a way that is embarrassing for an adult. In Latin, puer means boy. Puerile jokes, puerile arguments, puerile pranks: immaturity from people who should know better.

gre.s: The senator's opponents dismissed his insults as ____, the sort of schoolyard taunts unworthy of a serious political debate.
gre.clue: schoolyard taunts

en: Extremely idealistic in an unrealistic, impractical way
hook: QUIXOTIC comes from Don QUIXOTE, the knight who attacked windmills, thinking they were giants.
story: Quixotic. Rafi stood at a busy Dhaka intersection with a hand-painted sign: Please Take Turns. He believed that if he asked politely enough, every bus, car, and rickshaw would stop honking and wait patiently. The traffic swallowed him in minutes. His friends admired his heart, but called the plan quixotic. The word comes from Don Quixote, a dreamer who attacked windmills, thinking they were giants. Quixotic means noble but hopelessly unrealistic.

gre.s: Her colleagues admired her idealism but considered her plan to end world hunger within a decade ____, noble in aim yet wildly impractical.
gre.clue: noble in aim yet wildly impractical

en: A person who spends money wastefully
hook: SPEND-THRIFT: spends away all the thrift (savings).
story: Spendthrift. On the first day of every month, Tanvir's salary arrived. By the seventh, it was gone: new sneakers, restaurant dinners, a gaming headset he used twice. By the twentieth, he was borrowing money from his younger sister, who had saved half of her much smaller salary. "You are a spendthrift," she told him, counting out notes. A spendthrift spends money recklessly, wasting everything they have. The opposite is a miser, who refuses to spend at all.

gre.s: The heir was a notorious ____, squandering in three years a fortune that his frugal grandfather had spent decades accumulating.
gre.clue: squandering in three years a fortune

en: Habitually silent; saying very little
hook: TACIT-urn: tacit means unspoken. A person who keeps words unspoken.
story: Taciturn. Nadia's new roommate was a mystery. "How was your day?" "Fine." "Where are you from?" "Sylhet." "Do you like it here?" A nod. In one whole week, she said perhaps twenty words. She was not rude, just naturally quiet. Then one night Nadia heard her singing beautifully alone in the kitchen. Taciturn means habitually silent, saying very little. It is the opposite of loquacious. Tacit means unspoken; a taciturn person keeps most words unspoken.

gre.s: Known among reporters as ____, the general rarely granted interviews, and when he did, he answered most questions with a single word.
gre.clue: answered most questions with a single word

en: Cautious and alert about possible danger or problems
hook: WARY sounds like WORRY: you worry, so you're careful.
story: Wary. Sara once lost five thousand taka to a fake job advertisement that promised a high salary for easy work. Never again. Now, before accepting any offer, she checks the company's address, reads every line of the contract twice, and never, ever pays money upfront. Her friends call her suspicious; she calls it smart. Wary means cautious and alert to possible danger. Wary sounds like worry: you worry, so you watch carefully.

gre.s: Having been misled by flattering forecasts before, the investors were ____ of the startup's promise to triple its revenue within a year.
gre.clue: Having been misled by flattering forecasts before
